idiom_name: version attribute carried with the record + conditional write whose affected-row or compare-and-swap result is the stale-data test
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: store a strictly increasing version attribute next to the record's data; load it with the record; when writing, emit UPDATE ... SET version = version + 1, data = ? WHERE id = ? AND version = ? (or the store's equivalent conditional write) and test that exactly one row matched. Zero affected rows means the record changed since it was read - surface that as a conflict and let the caller re-read and retry, merge, or abort. Keep token maintenance in one owner (the mapper, repository or unit of work) so no statement can forget the predicate, and treat the token as opaque: never as identity, never as a domain attribute, never as an ordering key. For a shared in-process resource the same contract is an atomic compare-and-swap on the token, where a failed exchange hands back the current value for a re-read.
code_sketch:
load:  row = SELECT id, data, version FROM t WHERE id = ?
...edit...
write = UPDATE t SET data = ?, version = version + 1
          WHERE id = ? AND version = ?      # token read earlier
if affected_rows == 0: raise Conflict       # my copy is stale
# resolve: re-read, then merge / retry / fail -- never retry stale values
pitfalls: Forgetting the predicate on one write path (batch job, delete, admin fix) silently re-opens the lost update for every row that path touches.
Retrying without re-reading produces a write that overwrites exactly the change it conflicted with.
Incrementing the version outside the same atomic step as the data write loses the check the pattern depends on.
A timestamp token is poisoned by clock resolution and skew; a counter or database-generated rowversion is not.

Wrong move: one version token per fat aggregate under heavy concurrent writes -> every writer collides on the shared token even when editing disjoint fields, so throughput collapses into rollback-retry churn -> split the hot fields (counters, stock, tallies) into their own versioned sub-entity or row so each writer contends only on what it actually touches.

Wrong move: catching the conflict and retrying in an unbounded loop -> a hot row under sustained contention turns the retry loop into a CPU-burning storm that starves the workers -> cap retries (with a fresh read each attempt and backoff), then surface the conflict to the caller or fall back to a lock for that use case.
